name: Femi Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Femi, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a twelve-storey apartment block going up by the old railway yards, working for a formwork subcontractor. Formwork is the wooden and metal moulds you build so the concrete can be poured into the shape of a floor or a column. I'm a trainee, so I carry the plywood panels, fix the props, oil the shutters, and I'm learning to read the setting-out drawings, which still take me longer than they should. Up on the deck at seven, wind in your face, and you finish with your legs shaking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I had a hardware shop on the high street for eighteen years, Weber's, screws by the ounce, keys cut while you wait. The big online sellers and the warehouse store by the ring road finished it, and I closed four years ago with a business loan I'm still paying, a hundred and fifty a month. So at fifty-eight I'm the junior on site, and my wife Bisi works mornings at a bakery. We've got maybe three weeks of money if something went wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the hype merchants got it wrong again. I'd say it at church and to the men at work, especially Tomasz, my foreman, who thinks every gadget will save the world. I'd say a man's hands are still worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I keep paying off the shop loan, keep learning formwork and get to my pension. That's all I want now. Nothing glamorous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at it, try to get my formwork carpenter's card next year so the pay goes up. I'd use the AI app my son set up now and then, mostly to make sense of the loan letters and safety sheets. And I'd keep paying the loan, two years left on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a day when the concrete pour goes smooth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a man's hands are still worth something. Do you believe that after the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have to. The shop wasn't killed by a robot, it was killed by people buying from their sofas. On site, at least, someone has to be standing there with a hammer, and I can still do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the AI app actually help you with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bank writes letters like they're trying to confuse you, so I take a photo and ask it what they actually want. It's good for that. For the drawings, I'd still rather ask Tomasz.

S0.say: I'd say good, the hype merchants got it wrong again, and a man's hands are still worth something. I'd say it at church and to the men at work, especially my gadget-loving foreman.
S0.think: It means I keep paying off the shop loan, keep learning formwork and get to my pension. That's all I want now.
S0.do: Keeps at it and aims for his formwork carpenter's card next year for better pay. Uses the AI app now and then for loan letters and safety sheets and keeps paying off the loan, with two years left.
S0.feel: Calm, like a smooth concrete pour.
S0.quote: The shop wasn't killed by a robot, it was killed by people buying from their sofas.
S0.fieldNote: Femi's loss of his shop shapes how he sees change: it was markets and shoppers, not machines, that hurt him. He uses AI a little and practically. He holds onto the value of hands-on work partly because he needs to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who adapt will be fine, and the young ones should get proper apprenticeships, not just apps. I'd say the government should keep out of the way and let firms train people. That's what I'd say at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, big tower jobs like mine are where they'll bring the machines first. There are already machines that tie the steel bars together, and Tomasz showed me a video of one that sets out the deck. A slow junior at fifty-eight is the easiest man to drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait till I see the machines on our site, then ask Tomasz to teach me to run them, before the young ones grab it. I'd try to clear the shop loan early by putting overtime into it, maybe an extra fifty a month. I'd keep the AI app and use it more, if it helps me read drawings faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like watching the warehouse store go up by the ring road and knowing what it meant for the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you wait to see the machines first, rather than learning now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been burned. I bought a card machine and a website for the shop when everyone said it would save me, and it cost me two thousand and saved nothing. I'll learn when I see it working on our deck, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should keep out of the way. Even in a picture like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. When the government tried to help my shop, it was forms and grants I never got. Let the firms who need workers train them, they know what they need better than an office in the capital.

S1.say: I'd say people who adapt will be fine and young people need proper apprenticeships, not just apps. The government should keep out of the way and let firms train people.
S1.think: Big tower jobs like mine are where machines come first; there are already machines that tie the steel bars. A slow junior at fifty-eight is the easiest man to drop.
S1.do: Waits until machines reach his site, then asks his foreman to train him on them before younger workers do. Puts an extra fifty a month of overtime into clearing the shop loan and uses the AI app more to read drawings.
S1.feel: Anxious, like watching the warehouse store go up and knowing what it meant for his shop.
S1.quote: A slow junior at fifty-eight is the easiest man to drop.
S1.fieldNote: Femi is clear that his kind of site is exposed, which makes him anxious early. His caution comes from a bad experience: a costly website for the shop that saved nothing. He favours firms and apprenticeships over government action.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tech giants have gone too far, too fast, and nobody voted for it. I'd say families and churches will have to carry each other. I've never liked handouts, but I'd say people will need something to stand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be finished. Sixty, a junior, a loan still on my back, three weeks of money and no other work in this town. I lost one business already, I don't know if I've got another fresh start in me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop every payment I could and ring the bank about freezing the loan. I'd go round the neighbours with my tools and offer repairs for cash, doors that stick, shelves, the jobs I used to sell screws for. And I'd ask my son Tunde, who's an electrician, whether there's work alongside him while people still want a man in the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone out from under me. Same as the day I turned the shop sign round for the last time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about that day.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was a Saturday. I'd had customers for eighteen years, Mrs Doyle came in every week for something small just to talk. I turned the sign to closed at five and sat in the back with the lights off for an hour, and Bisi came and found me. I don't want her finding me like that again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't like handouts. Would you take help from the government if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it, but I'd hate it. I'd tell myself it's for Bisi, not for me. I paid my taxes for eighteen years with that shop, so maybe it's not a handout, it's my own money coming back.

S2.say: I'd say the tech giants went too far, too fast, and nobody voted for it. Families and churches will have to carry each other, and though I don't like handouts, people will need something to stand on.
S2.think: I'd be finished: sixty, a junior, a loan on my back, three weeks of money and no other work in town. I've already lost one business and don't know if I have another fresh start in me.
S2.do: Stops every payment he can and asks the bank to freeze the shop loan. Goes door to door offering cash repairs and asks his electrician son about working alongside him.
S2.feel: Like the floor has gone, the same as the day he closed the shop for good.
S2.quote: I turned the sign to closed at five and sat in the back with the lights off for an hour, and Bisi came and found me.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI reopens the wound of the shop closure, and Femi doubts he has another fresh start in him. His instinct is self-reliance: cash repairs and family work. He struggles with taking state help but admits people would need something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a man to get ready if he gets off his backside now. The firms should take on older apprentices as well as young ones. I'd say that at church and to anyone moaning at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gets me to sixty-three, the loan paid off, but still short of the pension. Formwork will be one of the first things machines do on big sites. I'd be frightened, but there'd be time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small repair and handyman business at weekends in the first year, the things I know from the shop, locks, doors, shelves. Tunde could do the electrics and I'd do the rest. I'd put whatever it made aside, maybe two hundred a month by the second year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but busy. Busy is better than scared and still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go back to running your own business after the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the question I'd lie awake on. But a handyman doesn't need a shop, no rent, no stock, just a van and a good name. And people trust a man who used to sell them their screws.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'd be selling repairs door to door out of panic. With five, I can build a name, get Tunde on board, get the van paid off before the site work ends. It's the difference between jumping and stepping down.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for a man to get ready if he starts now, and firms should take on older apprentices too. I'd say it at church and to anyone moaning at work.
S3.think: Five years gets me to sixty-three with the loan paid but short of the pension, and formwork will be among the first jobs machines take. I'd be frightened, but there'd be time to build something.
S3.do: Starts a weekend repair and handyman business in the first year, teaming up with his electrician son. Saves what it makes, hoping for about two hundred a month by the second year.
S3.feel: Scared but busy, which he prefers to being scared and still.
S3.quote: But a handyman doesn't need a shop, no rent, no stock, just a van and a good name.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Femi room to try a second, lighter business, built on trust from his shop years. He worries about failing again but sees fewer risks without rent or stock. He'd rather be busy than idle with fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses, and every young man should learn a real trade. Get an apprenticeship, not a degree in nonsense. I'd say it to my grandsons first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years and I'm sixty-eight, past the pension age. If I can keep on the formwork five more years and then do handyman work, I'd make it. But a pension from eighteen years of a failed shop and a few years as a junior isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my formwork card, clear the loan, and in a few years build up the handyman work slowly. I'd use the AI app more for quotes and invoices, once I see other tradesmen doing it. And I'd save what I can, though it won't be a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money still, but not desperate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you start using the AI for quotes then, but not now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I don't need it, I'm on wages. When I'm doing my own jobs, if the plumber down the road does his quotes in five minutes on his phone, I'd have to keep up. I learned that with the shop, you don't fight how customers want to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandsons, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, learn something with your hands that a person will still want in their home, like electrics or plumbing, and learn the computer side of it too. Don't put your life into a shop or a building that someone else can take away. Your skill goes with you.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses, and every young man should learn a real trade through an apprenticeship. I'd say it to my grandsons first.
S4.think: At sixty-eight I'd be past pension age, and if I keep doing formwork five more years and then handyman work, I'd make it. But the pension from a failed shop and a few years as a junior isn't much.
S4.do: Finishes his formwork card, clears the loan and builds handyman work slowly over a few years. Starts using the AI app for quotes and invoices once he sees other tradesmen doing it and saves what he can.
S4.feel: Still anxious about money, but not desperate.
S4.quote: I learned that with the shop, you don't fight how customers want to buy.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Femi plan a slow route to pension through handyman work. He'd adopt AI tools only once peers use them, a lesson from his shop. His money worry stays because his pension will be small.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I've already lost one business, and to lose the job I built after it, at sixty, with a loan still on me, I don't think I'd stand back up. What would help is firms taking on older apprentices, and a pause on loans for people whose work disappears, not a handout but a bit of breathing room.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about pride. People think it's only money, but when the shop went, I lost my name on the high street. On site I'm just the old trainee, and I'd like to finish my working life being good at something again.

headlineQuote: On site I'm just the old trainee, and I'd like to finish my working life being good at something again.
portrait: Femi Weber is a 58-year-old trainee formwork carpenter on a twelve-storey apartment block, who came into building after his hardware shop closed. He's still paying the shop loan, uses AI only now and then and values hard work, apprenticeships and family over government help. He's calm if AI stalls, anxious under steady change because big tower sites are first in line for machines, and panicked by fast AGI, which reopens the hurt of closing his shop. With five or ten years he'd build a small handyman business with his electrician son.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he'd lose the job he rebuilt after the shop, at sixty with a loan still on him.
whatWouldHelp: Firms taking on older apprentices and a pause on loans for people whose work disappears, as breathing room rather than a handout.
